stem: Money acts as an intermediate in the exchange process, and hence it is called a:
solution: Money acts as an intermediate in the exchange process, and hence it is called a medium of exchange; a person holding money can easily exchange it for any commodity or service.

stem: The system in which goods are directly exchanged for goods without the use of money is called the:
solution: The barter system is one where goods are directly exchanged for goods without the use of money; it requires a double coincidence of wants.

stem: In the barter system, both parties have to agree to sell and buy each other's commodities. This is called:
solution: In a barter system where money is not in use, double coincidence of wants is an essential feature — what a person desires to sell is exactly what the other wishes to buy. Money removes this difficulty by acting as a medium of exchange.

stem: Money solves the problem of double coincidence of wants because:
options: A person holding money can easily exchange it for any commodity or service that he or she might want
solution: Since money acts as a medium of exchange, everyone prefers to receive payments in money and then exchange the money for things they want; a person holding money can easily exchange it for any commodity or service, so both parties do not need to want each other's goods.

stem: Before the use of coins and paper money, a wide range of items served as money. Which of the following were used?
options: Grains and cattle in the earliest period, and later metallic coins — gold, silver, copper coins — right up to the last century
solution: Before the introduction of coins, a variety of objects was used as money, e.g., grains and cattle were used in the earliest period; thereafter metallic coins — gold, silver, copper coins — a phase which continued well into the last century.

stem: Modern forms of money — currency (paper notes and coins) — are without any use of their own. They are accepted as a medium of exchange because:
options: They are made of precious metal
The currency is authorised by the government of the country
solution: Modern currency is without any use of its own as a commodity; it is accepted as a medium of exchange because the currency is authorised by the government of the country.

stem: In India, the Reserve Bank of India issues currency notes on behalf of the:
solution: In India, the Reserve Bank of India issues currency notes on behalf of the central government; no other individual or organisation is allowed to issue currency.

stem: The law in India legalises the use of the rupee as a medium of payment that cannot be refused in settling transactions in India. The rupee is therefore called:
solution: The law legalises the use of rupee as a medium of payment that cannot be refused in settling transactions in India; no individual in India can legally refuse a payment made in rupees — hence the rupee is accepted as a medium of exchange, being legal tender.

stem: Modern forms of money include currency and:
solution: Modern forms of money include currency — paper notes and coins — and deposits with banks. People also hold money as deposits with banks, which can be withdrawn on demand.

stem: People deposit their extra cash with banks by opening a bank account in their name. Since these deposits can be withdrawn on demand, they are called:
solution: The deposits in bank accounts can be withdrawn on demand; these deposits are called demand deposits.

stem: Demand deposits share the essential features of money, so people can settle payments through them instead of cash by means of a:
solution: A cheque is a paper instructing the bank to pay a specific amount from the person's account to the person in whose name the cheque has been issued; demand deposits share the essential features of money, and payments can be made by cheque instead of cash.

stem: Since demand deposits are accepted widely as a means of payment, along with currency, they constitute:
solution: Since demand deposits are accepted widely as a means of payment, along with currency they constitute money in the modern economy.

stem: The facility of cheques against demand deposits makes it possible to directly settle payments without the use of:
solution: The facility of cheques against demand deposits makes it possible to directly settle payments without the use of cash; a cheque instructs the bank to pay from one account to another.

stem: Banks keep only a small proportion of their deposits as cash with themselves. In India, banks hold about what portion as cash?
options: Only about 15 per cent of their deposits as cash
solution: Banks in India these days hold about 15 per cent of their deposits as cash; this is kept as a provision to pay the depositors who might come to withdraw money from the bank on any given day.

stem: Banks use the major portion of the deposits to:
options: Extend loans to those who need money, for various economic activities
solution: Banks use the major portion of the deposits to extend loans; there is a huge demand for loans for various economic activities, so banks make use of the deposits to meet the loan requirements of the people.

stem: Banks make money by charging a higher interest rate on loans than what they offer on deposits. The difference between what is charged from borrowers and what is paid to depositors is the:
options: Main source of income of banks
solution: Banks charge a higher interest rate on loans than what they offer on deposits; the difference between what is charged from borrowers and what is paid to depositors is their main source of income.

stem: Banks mediate between those who have surplus funds (the depositors) and those who are in need of these funds (the borrowers). Banks are therefore called:
solution: A significant number of people deposit their money in banks; banks mediate between those who have surplus funds (the depositors) and those who are in need of these funds (the borrowers), acting as financial intermediaries.

stem: Credit (loan) refers to an agreement in which the lender supplies the borrower with money, goods or services in return for the promise of:
solution: Credit (loan) refers to an agreement in which the lender supplies the borrower with money, goods or services in return for the promise of future payment.

stem: The example of Salim (the shoe manufacturer) shows that credit helps him to meet the ongoing expenses of production, complete production on time, and thereby increase his earnings. This is credit that:
options: Plays a positive role, helping him to expand his business and earn more
solution: In the case of Salim, credit helps him meet the ongoing expenses of production, complete production in time and thereby increase his earnings; credit here plays a vital and positive role in development, helping the borrower expand and earn more.

stem: The example of Swapna (the farmer) who takes a loan for cultivation but suffers a crop failure due to pests illustrates that credit can push a borrower into a:
options: Debt-trap, forcing her to sell land to repay the loan, leaving her worse off
solution: In Swapna's case, the failure of the crop makes loan repayment impossible; she has to sell part of her land to repay the loan. Credit here pushes her into a debt-trap, leaving her worse off than before — showing credit can have a negative impact.

stem: Whether credit would be useful or not depends on the risks in the situation and whether there is some support in case of loss. The comparison of Salim and Swapna shows that credit's effect:
options: Depends on the situation — it can help or push into a debt trap, depending on the risks and outcomes
solution: Whether credit would be useful or not depends on the risks in the situation and whether there is some support in case of loss; in one situation credit helps increase earnings and is beneficial, while in another the person is caught in a debt-trap. So it is very important to consider the terms.

stem: In rural areas, the main demand for credit is for:
options: Crop production, which involves considerable costs on seeds, fertilisers, pesticides, water, electricity, etc.
solution: In rural areas, the main demand for credit is for crop production; crop production involves considerable costs on seeds, fertilisers, pesticides, water, electricity, repair of equipment, etc. There is a minimum stretch of three to four months between the time farmers buy inputs and sell the produce.

stem: Every loan agreement specifies an interest rate which the borrower must pay to the lender along with the repayment of the principal. In addition, lenders may demand:
solution: Every loan agreement specifies an interest rate which the borrower must pay to the lender along with the principal; lenders may also demand collateral (security) against loans.

stem: Collateral is an asset that the borrower owns (such as land, building, vehicle, livestock, deposits with banks) and uses as a guarantee to a lender until:
solution: Collateral is an asset that the borrower owns (such as land, building, vehicle, livestock, deposits with banks) and uses this as a guarantee to a lender until the loan is repaid. If the borrower fails to repay the loan, the lender has the right to sell the asset or collateral to obtain payment.

stem: The interest rate, collateral and documentation requirement, and the mode of repayment together comprise what are called:
solution: The interest rate, collateral and documentation requirement, and the mode of repayment together comprise what is called the terms of credit; these vary substantially from one credit arrangement to another.

stem: The terms of credit vary depending on the nature of the lender and the borrower. The two major categories of sources of credit are:
options: Formal sector loans and informal sector loans
solution: There are two major categories of sources of loans/credit: formal sector loans and informal sector loans. Among the former are banks and cooperatives; the informal lenders include moneylenders, traders, employers, relatives and friends.

stem: The Reserve Bank of India supervises the functioning of formal sources of loans. Which of the following does the RBI monitor?
options: That the banks actually maintain the cash balance and give loans not just to profit-making businesses but also to small cultivators, small-scale industries and small borrowers
solution: The RBI monitors the banks in actually maintaining the cash balance; it also sees that the banks give loans not just to profit-making businesses and traders but also to small cultivators, small-scale industries, and to small borrowers, etc. Banks have to submit information to the RBI on how much they are lending, to whom and at what interest rate.

stem: There is no organisation which supervises the credit activities of lenders in the informal sector. This means informal lenders:
options: Can charge whatever interest rate they wish, and there is no one to stop them from using unfair means to get their money back
solution: There is no organisation which supervises the credit activities of lenders in the informal sector; they can lend at whatever interest rate they choose. There is no one to stop them from using unfair means to get their money back.

stem: Compared to the formal sector, the informal sector lenders charge a much higher interest rate on loans. A higher cost of borrowing means:
options: A larger part of the earnings of the borrowers is used to repay the loan, leaving less income for themselves
solution: Most of the informal lenders charge a much higher interest on loans; thus, the cost to the borrower of informal loans is much higher. A higher cost of borrowing means a larger part of the earnings of the borrowers is used to repay the loan — in some cases the high interest rate can mean the amount to be repaid is greater than the borrower's total income, leading to a debt trap.

stem: The formal sources of credit provide loans at reasonable rates; hence the government must expand the formal sector to:
options: Break the monopoly of informal lenders, provide cheap and affordable credit especially to poor households, and support development
solution: It is necessary that banks and cooperatives increase their lending, particularly in rural areas, so that dependence on informal sources of credit reduces; cheap and affordable credit is crucial for the country's development. This would benefit poor households who otherwise depend on informal sources at high interest rates.

stem: Data shows that in urban areas, richer households take loans mostly from the formal sector, while poor households depend more on the:
solution: For the poor households in urban areas, the formal sector still meets only a small share of their credit needs — they take about 85 per cent of their loans from informal sources; the richer households, in contrast, take loans mostly from formal sources.

stem: It is important that the formal credit is distributed more equally so that:
options: The poor can benefit from cheaper loans, and everyone benefits from the higher incomes and lower dependence on informal lenders
solution: The poor households need to be provided greater access to formal credit; it is important that the formal credit is distributed more equally so that the poor can benefit from cheaper loans and are not exploited by informal lenders charging high interest.

stem: In recent years, people have tried out some newer ways of providing loans to the poor, especially through the idea of:
solution: In recent years, people have tried out some newer ways of providing loans to the poor; the idea is to organise rural poor, in particular women, into small Self-Help Groups (SHGs) and pool their savings.

stem: A typical Self-Help Group (SHG) has how many members who usually belong to one neighbourhood?
solution: A typical SHG has 15-20 members, usually belonging to one neighbourhood, who meet and save regularly. Saving per member varies from a few rupees to a few hundred rupees a month, depending on the ability of the people to save.

stem: In the Self-Help Group, most of the important decisions regarding the savings and loan activities are taken by:
solution: In an SHG, most of the important decisions regarding the savings and loan activities are taken by the group members. The group decides as regards the loans to be granted — the purpose, amount, interest rate, repayment schedule, and so on.

stem: The members of a Self-Help Group can take loans from the group's pooled savings to meet needs such as:
options: Releasing mortgaged land, meeting working capital needs (seeds, raw material), housing materials, and consumption needs
solution: Members can take small loans from the group itself to meet their needs — to release mortgaged land, for meeting working capital needs (e.g., buying seeds, fertilisers, raw materials), for acquiring assets like a sewing machine, for housing material, or for consumption needs.

stem: The Self-Help Groups help borrowers overcome the problem of the lack of collateral because:
options: They can get timely loans for a variety of purposes and at a reasonable interest rate without collateral; the group is the basis for bank loans
They give loans only to the rich
solution: SHGs help borrowers overcome the problem of lack of collateral; they can get timely loans for a variety of purposes and at a reasonable interest rate. Moreover, SHGs are the building blocks of organisation of the rural poor; not only do they help women become financially self-reliant, the regular meetings provide a platform to discuss and act on a variety of social issues.

stem: If the group is regular in savings, it becomes eligible for availing a loan from the:
solution: If the group is regular in saving, it becomes eligible for availing loans from the bank; the loan is sanctioned in the name of the group and is meant to create self-employment opportunities for the members.

stem: The most important reason SHGs are considered helpful for the poor is that they help to organise the poor and free them from the:
options: Clutches of informal lenders and the high interest and exploitation associated with them
solution: SHGs help the poor to organise, save, and access bank credit; this frees them from the clutches of informal lenders (moneylenders) who charge exorbitant interest and exploit the poor, thus helping the borrowers avoid the debt-trap.

stem: The Grameen Bank of Bangladesh, referred to in the chapter, is one of the biggest success stories in reaching the poor to provide them with credit. It was started by:
solution: The Grameen Bank of Bangladesh is one of the biggest success stories in reaching the poor to meet their credit needs at reasonable rates; it started as a small project and was founded by Nobel Peace Prize winner Muhammad Yunus.

stem: Almost all the borrowers of the Grameen Bank of Bangladesh are:
options: Women who belong to the poorest sections of society
solution: The Grameen Bank of Bangladesh has over nine million members in about 81,600 villages; almost all the borrowers are women and belong to the poorest sections of society. These borrowers have proved that not only are poor women reliable borrowers, but they can start and run a variety of small income-generating activities successfully.

stem: The formal sector still meets only about half of the total credit needs of the rural people. Which body needs to lend more, especially to small borrowers?
solution: The formal sector still meets only about half of the total credit needs of the rural people; banks and cooperative societies need to lend more, particularly in rural areas and to small borrowers, so that dependence on informal sources reduces.

stem: The main reason why the poor are still dependent on informal sources of credit is that:
options: Banks are not present everywhere in rural India, and where present they demand collateral and documentation which the poor may not have
solution: The poor still depend on informal sources because banking has not spread to all rural areas, and even where banks are present, they require proper documents and collateral, which poor households often lack. Absence of collateral is one of the major reasons which prevents the poor from getting bank loans.

stem: The two important channels through which cheap credit can reach the rural poor, as highlighted in the chapter, are:
solution: Cheap credit can reach the rural poor mainly through expanded lending by banks and cooperatives (the formal sector) and through Self-Help Groups (SHGs), which pool savings and access bank loans, freeing the poor from exploitative informal lenders.

stem: One of the main reasons for the government/RBI to insist that a share of bank loans go to small borrowers is to:
options: Ensure that credit reaches the poor and productive sectors of the economy, supporting balanced development
solution: The RBI ensures that banks give loans not just to profit-making businesses and traders but also to small cultivators, small-scale industries and small borrowers; this ensures that credit reaches all sections, especially the poor and productive sectors, promoting balanced and inclusive development.

stem: Cheap and affordable credit is crucial for the country's development because:
options: It enables people to undertake productive activities, expand businesses, increase incomes and thereby contribute to economic growth
solution: Cheap and affordable credit is crucial for the country's development; when people can borrow at reasonable rates, they can invest in crop production, set up small businesses, and expand economic activities, which increases their incomes and contributes to overall economic growth.

stem: Which of the following correctly distinguishes formal from informal credit?
options: Formal sources charge higher interest than informal
Formal sources (banks, cooperatives) are supervised by the RBI and charge lower interest; informal sources (moneylenders, traders) are unsupervised and charge higher interest
Informal sources are supervised by the RBI
solution: Formal sources of credit (banks and cooperatives) are supervised by the RBI, charge lower interest rates, and follow terms of credit; informal sources (moneylenders, traders, employers, relatives) are unsupervised, can charge very high interest, and often exploit borrowers.

stem: The essential idea behind a Self-Help Group's ability to get bank loans without collateral is:
options: The group's regular savings and collective responsibility (peer support and shared accountability) substitute for individual collateral
solution: In SHGs, the group's regular savings record and the collective responsibility of members (peer pressure and mutual accountability) serve as a substitute for individual collateral; banks lend to the group, and the members ensure repayment, overcoming the poor's lack of collateral.

stem: The overall message of the chapter 'Money and Credit' is that:
options: Money removes the difficulties of barter, and credit can play a positive role in development if provided on reasonable terms through the formal sector and SHGs, but exploitative informal credit can trap the poor in debt
solution: The chapter concludes that money overcomes the double-coincidence problem of barter, and credit is crucial for development; whether credit helps or harms depends on its terms. Expanding cheap, formal credit (banks, cooperatives, SHGs) to the poor is essential, while unregulated informal credit at high interest can push the poor into a debt-trap.

stem: The difficulty in the barter system, where both parties must want to buy and sell each other's goods, is called the:
solution: In the barter system, both parties have to agree to sell and buy each other's commodities; this necessity is called double coincidence of wants, which money eliminates by acting as an intermediary.

stem: Money is often called a 'medium of exchange' because it:
options: Acts as an intermediate in the exchange process
solution: Money acts as an intermediate in the exchange process, so it is called a medium of exchange; a person holding money can easily exchange it for any commodity or service.

stem: In India, currency notes are issued by the:
solution: In India, the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) issues currency notes on behalf of the central government; no other individual or organisation is allowed to issue currency.

stem: Modern currency is accepted as a medium of exchange because it is:
options: Authorised by the government of the country
solution: Modern currency has no value of its own as a commodity; it is accepted because it is authorised by the government of the country, which declares the rupee as legal tender.

stem: The deposits in bank accounts that can be withdrawn on demand are called:
solution: People's extra cash deposited in bank accounts that they can withdraw as and when they require are called demand deposits; these share the essential features of money.

stem: A cheque is:
options: A paper instructing the bank to pay a specific amount from a person's account
solution: A cheque is a paper instructing the bank to pay a specific amount from the person's account to the person in whose name the cheque has been drawn, enabling payment without cash.

stem: Banks keep only a small proportion of their deposits as cash reserves because:
options: Only a fraction of depositors withdraw at any one time
solution: Banks keep only about 15 per cent of their deposits as cash, since on any given day only some depositors come to withdraw; the rest is used to extend loans, meeting the credit needs of the economy.

stem: Banks earn their income mainly by:
options: Charging a higher interest on loans than they pay on deposits
solution: Banks charge a higher rate of interest on loans than what they pay on deposits; the difference between the two is the main source of the banks' income.

stem: Credit (a loan) refers to an agreement in which the lender supplies the borrower with money, goods or services in return for:
solution: Credit refers to an agreement in which the lender supplies the borrower with money, goods or services in return for the promise of future payment, usually with interest.

stem: An asset (like land, building or deposits) that a borrower pledges to a lender as a guarantee until the loan is repaid is called:
solution: Collateral is an asset that the borrower owns (such as land, building, vehicle or deposits) and uses as a guarantee to the lender until the loan is repaid; if the borrower fails to repay, the lender can sell it.

stem: The interest rate, collateral requirement, documentation and the mode of repayment together are called the:
solution: The interest rate, collateral and documentation requirement, and the mode of repayment together comprise the terms of credit, which vary depending on the nature of the lender and the borrower.

stem: The example of Salim, the shoe manufacturer, is used to show that credit can:
options: Help increase production and earnings when the situation is favourable
solution: Salim uses credit to meet the working capital needs of production, complete a large order on time, and earn more; this shows that in a favourable situation, credit helps increase incomes and better off.

stem: The example of Swapna, the farmer who falls into a debt trap after crop failure, shows that credit can:
options: Push a borrower into a worse situation when there is a high risk of failure
solution: Swapna's crop fails and she is unable to repay her loan, forcing her to sell part of her land; this shows that credit in high-risk situations can push a person into a debt trap and make things worse.

stem: The formal sources of credit in India are supervised by the:
solution: Formal sector loans — from banks and cooperatives — are supervised by the Reserve Bank of India, which monitors that the banks actually maintain cash balances and give loans fairly, including to small borrowers.

stem: There is no organisation that supervises the credit activities of the informal lenders, so they:
options: Can charge whatever interest rate they wish
solution: No one supervises the credit activities of informal lenders like moneylenders and traders; they can lend at whatever interest rate they choose, and there is no one to prevent them from using unfair means.

stem: Compared to the formal sector, informal-sector lenders usually charge:
options: A much higher rate of interest
solution: The informal lenders charge a much higher interest rate on loans than the formal sector; a higher cost of borrowing means a larger part of the earnings of the borrowers is used to repay the loan.

stem: A Self-Help Group (SHG) typically consists of how many members?
solution: A typical Self-Help Group consists of 15-20 members, usually belonging to one neighbourhood, who meet and save regularly.

stem: In a Self-Help Group, decisions regarding the savings and loan activities are taken by:
solution: In the SHG, most of the important decisions regarding the savings and loan activities are taken by the group members; the group decides the loans to be granted, the purpose, amount, interest and repayment schedule.

stem: A major advantage of Self-Help Groups is that they help poor borrowers overcome the problem of:
solution: SHGs help the poor obtain loans without the collateral demanded by banks; the group's savings and its collective responsibility act as the guarantee, so the poor can access credit.

stem: The Grameen Bank of Bangladesh, referred to in the chapter, is famous for providing credit to:
options: The poor, especially poor women, without collateral
solution: The Grameen Bank of Bangladesh, started by Muhammad Yunus, is one of the biggest success stories in reaching the poor to meet their credit needs at reasonable rates; almost all its borrowers are women from poor households.

stem: Assertion (A): The poor often depend on informal sources of credit. Reason (R): They lack the collateral and documents required by banks for formal loans.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
solution: The poor frequently borrow from moneylenders because banks require collateral and paperwork they cannot provide; hence the absence of collateral pushes them to costly informal credit — R explains A.

stem: Assertion (A): It is necessary to expand formal-sector credit to rural areas. Reason (R): Formal credit is cheaper and free from the exploitation of high informal interest rates.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
solution: Expanding formal credit is important because it charges lower interest and is supervised, freeing borrowers from the debt traps caused by exploitative informal lenders — R explains A.

stem: Data shows that in urban areas, richer households take most of their loans from:
solution: Studies show that richer urban households obtain most of their credit from formal sources, whereas poorer households depend heavily on informal sources, revealing unequal access to cheap credit.

stem: The formal sector meets only about __________ of the total credit needs of the rural people.
solution: The formal sector still meets only about half of the total credit needs of the rural people; the remaining credit comes from informal sources at high cost, so formal credit must be expanded.

stem: Match the source with its type: (i) Commercial bank (ii) Moneylender (iii) Cooperative society — (a) informal (b) formal (c) formal:
solution: Commercial banks and cooperative societies are formal sources of credit, while moneylenders are informal sources.

stem: Cooperative societies are one of the major sources of cheap credit in rural areas; they provide loans by:
options: Pooling members' resources and accepting deposits, then lending to members
solution: Members of a cooperative pool their resources for cooperation; they accept deposits and in turn provide loans to members at reasonable rates, and may also obtain funds from banks to lend further.

stem: Cheap and affordable credit is crucial for the country's development because it:
options: Helps people set up businesses, increase production and improve incomes
solution: Cheap and affordable credit lets people establish and expand businesses, invest in agriculture and industry, increase production, and raise their incomes, thereby contributing to the country's development.

stem: Whether credit will be useful or push someone into a debt trap depends largely on:
options: The risks in the situation and whether there is support in case of loss
solution: Whether credit helps or harms depends on the risks in the situation and whether there is some support in case of loss; in a favourable situation credit helps, but in a risky one it can lead to a debt trap.

stem: The main demand for credit in rural areas is for:
solution: In rural areas, the main demand for credit is for crop production, which involves considerable costs on seeds, fertilisers, pesticides, water and so on; farmers usually repay after the harvest.

stem: One reason the government/RBI insists that banks give a share of loans to small borrowers is to:
options: Ensure that poor and small borrowers also benefit from cheap formal credit
solution: The RBI requires banks to lend not just to profit-making businesses but also to small cultivators, small-scale industries and small borrowers, so that the benefits of cheap formal credit reach all sections.

stem: A Self-Help Group becomes eligible to avail loans from a bank when it:
options: Has been regular in saving over a period
solution: If a Self-Help Group is regular in its savings, it becomes eligible for availing a loan from the bank; the loan is sanctioned in the name of the group and is meant to create self-employment opportunities.

stem: The essential idea behind an SHG's ability to get a bank loan without collateral is:
options: The group's collective savings and mutual responsibility act as a guarantee
solution: SHGs can get bank loans without individual collateral because the group's regular savings and the collective (joint) responsibility of members to repay serve as the guarantee to the bank.

stem: Self-Help Groups also help rural women by:
options: Enabling them to save, borrow and become self-reliant and organised
solution: SHGs help women become financially self-reliant; the regular meetings provide a platform to discuss and act on social issues such as health, nutrition and domestic violence too.

stem: The two important channels through which cheap institutional credit reaches rural areas are cooperatives and:
solution: Cheap institutional (formal) credit reaches the rural people mainly through cooperative societies and commercial banks, both of which are supervised and lend at reasonable rates.

stem: Modern forms of money, such as currency and deposits, are closely linked with the working of the:
solution: Modern money — currency and demand deposits — is closely connected with the modern banking system, since banks accept deposits, make payments through cheques, and provide loans.

stem: Money as a medium of exchange removes the need for:
solution: By acting as a medium of exchange, money removes the need for a double coincidence of wants — a person can sell goods for money and use that money to buy whatever they need, from anyone.

stem: Demand deposits are considered a form of money because they:
options: Can be used to make payments (e.g. by cheque) just like cash
solution: Demand deposits share the essential features of money: since payments can be made through cheques against them and they are widely accepted, demand deposits are considered money along with currency.

stem: A high cost of borrowing from informal lenders means that:
options: A large part of the borrower's earnings is used to repay the loan
solution: When interest rates are very high, a much larger part of the borrower's income goes towards repayment; little is left for the borrower, sometimes leading to a debt trap.

stem: The formal credit sector is important also because loans from it are given at:
options: Reasonable, lower interest rates than informal sources
solution: Formal sources of credit (banks and cooperatives) provide loans at reasonable, lower interest rates than informal lenders, which is why extending formal credit reduces the burden on borrowers.

stem: Before coins and paper money, various items served as money; these are examples of:
solution: Before the introduction of coins and paper currency, a wide range of items — grain, cattle, shells and metals — served as money; these are called commodity money.

stem: The reason a debt trap occurs is that:
options: The borrower's income is too low to repay the loan and interest, forcing further borrowing or asset sale
solution: A debt trap arises when a borrower, unable to repay the loan and its high interest from insufficient income, has to borrow again or sell assets like land, worsening their situation.

stem: The banks act as a link (intermediary) between:
options: Depositors with surplus funds and borrowers who need funds
Buyers and sellers of goods only
solution: Banks mediate between those who have surplus funds (depositors) and those who are in need of these funds (borrowers), channelling savings into productive loans.

stem: Which of the following best distinguishes formal from informal credit?
options: Formal credit is supervised by the RBI and charges lower interest; informal is unsupervised and costlier
solution: Formal credit (banks, cooperatives) is supervised by the RBI and charges reasonable interest, while informal credit (moneylenders, traders) is unsupervised and usually charges much higher interest.

stem: Cooperative societies are one of the major sources of cheap credit in rural areas. Members of a cooperative pool their resources for cooperation in certain areas; they accept deposits and in turn:
options: Charge very high interest like moneylenders
Grant loans to members at a reasonable rate of interest for purchase of agricultural inputs, cattle, fishing nets, etc.
solution: Cooperative societies are one of the major sources of cheap credit in rural areas; members pool their resources, accept deposits from members, and if funds are needed they borrow from banks. These funds are used to provide loans to members at a reasonable rate of interest for the purchase of agricultural inputs, cattle, vehicles, construction, and other needs, freeing them from dependence on moneylenders.
